Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Houston Astros shortstop Miguel Tejada is expected to plead guilty Wednesday in federal court to a count of lying to Congress about his knowledge of Major League Baseball players using performance-enhancing drugs, according to officials familiar with the case. Miguel Tejada, a shortstop for the Houston Astros, has been charged with lying to Congress. In a document filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, Tejada is charged in a criminal "information," a document that routinely signals a plea bargain agreement. The document does not directly accuse Tejada of using steroids or other substances. However, the court document says that in 2003 Tejada gave another player more than $5,000 in checks "for substances which he believed to be HGH [human growth hormone]." The document says Tejada lied to congressional investigators when he told them on August 26, 2005, that he had never heard discussions about steroids by other players, and that he never knew of any other player using steroids. After the December 2007 Mitchell Report on steroid use in baseball, which appeared to contradict Tejada, the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform asked the Justice Department to investigate whether Tejada "made knowingly false statements to the committee." The investigators concluded he had lied. "Defendant Tejada unlawfully withheld pertinent information from the committee because defendant Tejada before and during his interview with the committee staff, then and there well knew that Player #1 [unidentified], one of his teammates on the Oakland Athletics, had used steroids and HGH," the document says. Tejada played for the Athletics from 1997 to 2003. He is scheduled to appear at 11 a.m. Wednesday before a magistrate judge, indicating the charge against him will be a misdemeanor carrying a maximum sentence of a year in jail. However, a government official familiar with the case said that under sentencing guidelines, Tejada could get from zero to 6 months, which means he may receive probation without jail time. Tejada, who started his MLB career in 1997, hit at least 30 home runs from 2000 through 2004 with the exception of 2003, when he hit 27. He won the American League's most valuable player award in 2002, when he hit a career-best 34 home runs. He matched that total in 2004, his first year with the Baltimore Orioles. He began playing with Houston in 2008. The information came one day after MLB star Alex Rodriguez -- the New York Yankees' third baseman since 2004 -- admitted that he had used a "banned substance" during the 2001-2003 seasons. Sports Illustrated had reported that Rodriguez had tested positive for steroids in 2003, when he was playing for the Texas Rangers.

# Astros shortstop Miguel Tejada charged with lying to Congress

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Houston Astros shortstop Miguel Tejada has been charged with lying to congressional investigators about his knowledge of performance-enhancing drug use in Major League Baseball, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

A criminal information filed in U.S. District Court in Washington charges Tejada with one count of making false statements to Congress during a 2005 interview with House committee staff.

Prosecutors allege Tejada denied knowing that another player had used steroids or discussed performance-enhancing drugs. Authorities said Tejada had previously learned of steroid use by a former teammate and had conversations about the subject.

The charge does not accuse Tejada of using steroids himself.

Tejada, a six-time All-Star and the 2002 American League Most Valuable Player, is expected to plead guilty. The misdemeanor charge carries a maximum penalty of one year in prison, although federal sentencing guidelines could call for a lesser punishment.

The congressional interview was part of a wider investigation into steroid use in professional baseball. Lawmakers had been examining whether players and league officials were truthful about the prevalence of banned substances in the sport.

Major League Baseball and the Houston Astros did not immediately announce disciplinary action against Tejada.

The case adds Tejada to a growing list of prominent baseball figures drawn into federal investigations involving steroids, human growth hormone and statements made under oath or to government investigators.

# Miguel Tejada charged with making false statements to Congress over performance-enhancing drugs

**WASHINGTON —** Major League Baseball star Miguel Tejada was charged Tuesday with making false statements to congressional investigators about his knowledge of another player’s use of steroids and human growth hormone, according to a criminal information filed in federal court.

The misdemeanor charge stems from an August 2005 interview in which congressional staff questioned Tejada as part of an investigation into performance-enhancing drugs in baseball. Prosecutors allege that Tejada falsely denied having discussed steroids or human growth hormone with a former teammate, even though that player had allegedly told Tejada about his own drug use and supplied Tejada with performance-enhancing substances.

The filing in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia charges Tejada with one count of making misrepresentations to Congress under federal law. The use of a criminal information rather than an indictment generally signals that a defendant has agreed to waive indictment and may be preparing to enter a plea.

Tejada, a six-time All-Star and the 2002 American League Most Valuable Player, was playing for the Houston Astros at the time of the charge.

## Alleged false denial during congressional interview

Congressional investigators interviewed Tejada on Aug. 26, 2005, amid scrutiny of testimony given earlier that year by Baltimore Orioles teammate Rafael Palmeiro. Palmeiro had emphatically denied using steroids during a nationally televised House hearing in March but later tested positive for a banned substance.

During the August interview, investigators asked Tejada about his knowledge of steroid use by other major-league players. According to the court filing, Tejada said he had never discussed steroids with the player identified by prosecutors and had never been told that the player was using steroids or human growth hormone.

“I never had a conversation with him about steroids,” Tejada said, according to the filing. “I never asked him for steroids.”

Prosecutors contend those statements were knowingly false.

Although the charging document did not identify the former teammate by name, the allegations correspond to information involving Adam Piatt, who played with Tejada on the Oakland Athletics and was later interviewed for former Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell’s investigation into performance-enhancing drugs in baseball.

The charge does not accuse Tejada of lying under oath at a public congressional hearing. Instead, it concerns allegedly false statements made during a transcribed interview with congressional staff. Federal law prohibits knowingly and willfully making materially false statements in matters within the jurisdiction of the legislative branch.

## Mitchell Report detailed Piatt’s allegations

Mitchell’s report, released in December 2007, said Piatt told investigators that he had discussed performance-enhancing drugs with Tejada while the two were teammates in Oakland.

According to the report, Piatt said Tejada asked him what substances he was using and then requested the same materials. Piatt told Mitchell’s investigators that he supplied Tejada with testosterone and human growth hormone.

The report also cited two checks from Tejada to Piatt—one for **$3,100** and another for **$3,200**—that investigators viewed as corroborating Piatt’s account. The checks were written in 2003, according to the report.

Piatt said he initially believed the money was intended to help him during a difficult financial period, but later understood that the payments covered the substances he obtained for Tejada. Mitchell’s investigators reported that they had reviewed copies of the checks.

The Mitchell Report presented Piatt’s statements as allegations based on his account and supporting records; it was not a judicial finding that Tejada had used steroids or human growth hormone. Tejada was not charged Tuesday with possessing or using performance-enhancing drugs. The criminal case focuses on whether he knowingly lied to congressional investigators about conversations and transactions involving them.

## Questions arose after Palmeiro suspension

Tejada’s congressional interview took place against the backdrop of Palmeiro’s suspension for a positive steroid test.

After the suspension, Palmeiro reportedly suggested that a vitamin B-12 injection provided by Tejada might have caused the positive result. Tejada said the substance was vitamin B-12, which was commonly used by some players as an energy supplement and was not prohibited by Major League Baseball.

Congressional staff subsequently questioned Tejada about the injection and about his broader knowledge of drug use in baseball. The government’s new case, however, centers on his answers concerning the former Oakland teammate described in the Mitchell Report—not on an allegation that Tejada intentionally gave Palmeiro a banned substance.

## Filing points toward expected court appearance

Because prosecutors proceeded through a criminal information, Tejada was expected to appear promptly in federal court to respond to the charge. Such filings are often made after plea negotiations, though the document itself does not constitute a conviction.

The case marks another significant legal development arising from Congress’s investigation of steroid use in professional baseball. Several prominent players have faced scrutiny over whether their statements to lawmakers or federal investigators were truthful, even when the underlying use of performance-enhancing drugs did not itself result in criminal charges.

Tejada’s prosecution also underscores a distinction that federal authorities have repeatedly emphasized: witnesses may decline to answer certain questions or invoke legal rights, but they may not knowingly give materially false information to Congress.

Neither the allegations in the criminal information nor those in the Mitchell Report amount to a finding of guilt. Prosecutors will have to establish—or Tejada will have to admit in a guilty plea—that his statements were false, that he knew they were false and that they were material to the congressional investigation.
